lessons.title: RBI Intervention and Forex Reserves: How India Manages Volatility

children.text: In FY26, RBI sold a net $53.13 billion in the spot forex market, the most it has ever sold in a single year. By the end of July 2026, it had also promised to sell another $136.77 billion in future dates through forward contracts. And yet, in the week ended 4 September 2026, India's forex reserves hit a record $785.7 billion. How can a central bank sell record amounts of dollars and still end up with record reserves? The answer tells you exactly how RBI manages the rupee, what its reserves really are, and why it slows the rupee's fall instead of trying to stop it.

body.text: RBI is a shock absorber, not a wall. Its reserves buy time and calm panic, but the rupee's direction is still set by the big three forces. Anyone betting that RBI will hold a particular level forever is misreading the job RBI says it is doing.

children.text: What India's Forex Reserves Actually Are

markDefs.definition: Special Drawing Rights. An international reserve asset created by the IMF, valued against a basket of major currencies and allocated to member countries.
Forex reserves expressed as the number of months of imports they could pay for. A common measure of how safe a country's external position is.

children.text: Forex reserves are not a pile of dollar notes in a Mumbai vault. Most of the money sits in foreign government bonds, deposits with other central banks and the Bank for International Settlements, plus gold,
and India's reserve position at the IMF. RBI reports the total every Friday. Policymakers usually judge its size by
, and RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has repeatedly said India's reserves can cover about 11 months of imports.

body.title: India's Forex Reserves, Week Ended 4 September 2026 ($ billion)

children.text: Foreign currency assets make up about 82% of the total. They are held in several currencies, mainly dollars, euros, pounds and yen, but are reported in dollars. That creates a quirk: when the dollar strengthens, the euro and yen holdings are worth fewer dollars, so reserves can fall even if RBI has not sold a single dollar. The same happens with gold when its price drops. Always ask whether a change in reserves came from intervention or from valuation.

body.title: India's Forex Reserves at Key Points ($ billion)
The 2022 drawdown
body.prompt: India's reserves were $642.45 billion in September 2021 and $524.52 billion in October 2022. By what percentage did they fall? Enter a positive number rounded to two decimals.
body.explanation: 524.52 ÷ 642.45 minus 1 = minus 18.36%. About $118 billion disappeared in a year. Part of it was RBI selling dollars to slow the rupee's slide past 80 and 83. Part of it was valuation loss, because a surging dollar shrank the dollar value of RBI's euro, yen and gold holdings.

body.caption: How RBI steps into the forex market

cells: Spot intervention
Sells or buys dollars for delivery in two days, usually through state-run banks
Immediate impact on the rupee
Uses reserves now and drains or adds rupee liquidity in banks
Forward intervention
Agrees today to sell or buy dollars on future dates
Eases pressure without spending reserves today
Creates future dollar commitments that must be honoured
Buy/sell swaps
Buys dollars from banks now and sells them back later, or the reverse
Adjusts rupee liquidity while managing reserves
Reverses at maturity
Offshore NDF action
Sells dollars in the NDF market through banks
Calms offshore pressure before India opens
Settled in dollars at fixing
Regulatory measures
Position caps, NDF curbs, rules on rebooking contracts
Cuts speculation quickly
Can disrupt hedging and invite criticism
Inflow schemes
Swap windows for FCNR(B) deposits and foreign borrowing
Pulls in fresh dollars
RBI bears some cost through concessional swap rates

stats.label: Net spot dollar sales, FY26
stats.context: A record, up from $34.51 billion in FY25

stats.label: Net short forward position
stats.context: Record, end of July 2026, up from $103.33 billion in June

children.text: Now the opening puzzle makes sense. RBI sold heavily in the spot market and shifted much of its intervention into forwards, which do not reduce reserves until they mature. Then, from June 2026, a swap window for FCNR(B) deposits pulled in so many dollars that RBI closed it a month early, on 31 August. Add valuation gains, and reported reserves rose to a record even while RBI was defending the rupee.

body.title: The hidden side effect: selling dollars soaks up rupees

markDefs.definition: Offsetting the effect of forex intervention on domestic money supply, for example by injecting rupees through bond purchases or swaps after selling dollars.

children.text: When RBI sells dollars, banks pay for them in rupees. Those rupees leave the banking system, which tightens liquidity and can push up short-term interest rates, even if RBI has not touched the repo rate. To prevent this, RBI often injects rupees back through bond purchases, buy/sell swaps or other operations. This is called
. It is one reason RBI leaned more on forwards and swaps in FY26: they manage the rupee without draining as much cash from banks today.

content.caption: Every dollar RBI sells in the spot market removes rupees from the banking system

body.title: Liquidity drained
body.prompt: Suppose RBI sells $11.88 billion in the spot market in one month at an average USD/INR rate of 95.50 (an illustrative rate). How many crore rupees does this drain from the banking system? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: $11.88 billion × 95.50 = ₹1,134.54 billion. One crore is 10 million, so ₹1,134.54 billion = ₹1,13,454 crore. That is a large chunk of banking liquidity, which is why spot intervention on this scale usually comes with liquidity-injecting operations.

body.text: Read the headline reserve number with care. At the end of July 2026, RBI's net short forward position was $136.77 billion, dollars it has already promised to deliver in future, with $15.59 billion due within one month. Subtracting it from the September reserve figure is only a rough comparison, because the dates differ, but it suggests the reserves RBI can freely use are meaningfully smaller than the headline $785.7 billion.

children.text: Smoothing Volatility vs Defending a Level

markDefs.definition: An IMF classification where the exchange rate stays within a 2% band around a trend for at least six months. India was placed in this category in November 2025.

children.text: RBI's stated policy is that the market sets the rupee's level and RBI intervenes only to curb excessive volatility. The IMF judges regimes by behaviour, not statements. After labelling India a "stabilised arrangement" in 2023, it reclassified India as a

in November 2025: the rupee is allowed to weaken gradually along a trend, but sharp moves are smoothed out. That matches what traders see on screens: slow, steady depreciation with sudden spikes capped.

body.title: Two ways a central bank can use its reserves

columns.label: Smoothing volatility (RBI's approach)
points: Lets the trend play out and slows the pace
Uses reserves in bursts, then rebuilds them when inflows return
Leaves no fixed line for speculators to attack

columns.label: Defending a fixed level
points: Promises a specific rate no matter what
Burns reserves continuously when the trend is against it
Gives speculators a clear target to bet against
Can end in a sudden, forced devaluation, as in several emerging-market crises

body.text: Defending a level against the fundamentals can end badly. Sri Lanka spent much of its reserves trying to hold its currency before a crisis in 2022 forced a sharp devaluation and a sovereign debt default. India itself had reserves for only a few weeks of imports in 1991. RBI's large reserves today exist precisely so it never has to fight that battle, which is also why it will not spend them all to protect one number.

events.title: Gold pledged in a crisis
events.description: With reserves nearly exhausted, India pledges about 47 tonnes of gold with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to raise emergency funds.

events.title: FCNR(B) swap window
events.description: RBI's concessional swap windows draw in about $34 billion and end the taper tantrum slide.

events.title: Reserves drawn down
events.description: Reserves fall to about $524.5 billion after a year of heavy selling and valuation losses as the rupee crosses 80 and 83.

events.title: Large buy/sell swaps
events.description: During a severe banking liquidity squeeze, RBI runs a $5 billion six-month dollar-rupee buy/sell swap in January and a $10 billion three-year swap in February to inject rupees.

events.title: IMF says crawl-like
events.description: The IMF reclassifies India's exchange rate regime as a crawl-like arrangement.

events.title: Record spot selling
events.description: RBI net sells $53.13 billion in the spot market, its highest ever for a financial year.

events.title: Regulatory tools
events.description: RBI caps banks' net open rupee positions and curbs NDF activity to break onshore-offshore arbitrage.

events.title: Rebuilding reserves
events.description: A new FCNR(B) swap window pulls in strong inflows and is closed early on 31 August. Reserves reach a record $785.7 billion in the week ended 4 September.

body.title: RBI's stated goal
body.question: Which statement best describes RBI's stated approach to the rupee?
options: RBI fixes USD/INR at a target level and defends it
RBI never intervenes and lets the rupee float freely
RBI lets the market set the level and intervenes to curb excessive volatility
RBI aims to keep the rupee weak to help exporters
body.explanation: RBI's consistent position is that it does not target a level and steps in only to smooth excessive volatility. The IMF's crawl-like classification reflects that in practice the rupee moves gradually along a trend with sharp swings capped.

body.title: Betting on the RBI floor
body.scenario: USD/INR has jumped from 95.50 to 97.00 in three trading days after a crude spike and heavy FPI selling. Each time it touches 97.00, dealers report state-run banks selling dollars and the rupee bounces back to 96.80. Vikram manages treasury for an Ahmedabad chemicals exporter with $500,000 of receivables due in two months, and he has already hedged them by selling USD/INR futures. Now, with USD/INR at 96.90, he wants to sell another $1 million of futures, beyond anything the company is owed, reasoning that "RBI will never let it go past 97, so this is free money."
body.prompt: Evaluate Vikram's plan using what you learned about RBI's approach, its reserves and forward book, the big three forces and the rules on rupee derivatives. What could go wrong, and what would a more disciplined approach look like?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The extra $1 million has no underlying exposure behind it. Rupee-pair contracts on NSE and BSE may be used only to hedge a genuine exposure, so this top-up is speculation the rules do not permit, even though it is below $100 million and needs no documents.
2. RBI's stated goal is to curb volatility, not to defend 97.00. Repeated selling at 97 shows RBI slowing a fast move, not promising a ceiling.
3. The forces behind the move, crude and FPI outflows, have not reversed. If they persist, RBI is likely to step back and let the rupee adjust gradually, consistent with a crawl-like regime. RBI's usable firepower is also smaller than headline reserves suggest because of its large forward commitments.
4. His existing hedge is doing its job: any loss on those futures is offset by more rupees on the receivables. The extra position has no such offset. If 97 breaks and USD/INR runs to 98, it loses about $1,000,000 × 1.10 = ₹11,00,000, debited day by day through mark-to-market.
5. A disciplined approach: keep the hedge matched to the company's real exposure, treat intervention levels as speed bumps rather than floors, and adjust the hedge only as receivables change, instead of betting the company's money on RBI.

body.title: The IMF's label
body.textWithBlank: In November 2025, the IMF reclassified India's exchange rate regime as a ___ arrangement.
body.explanation: A crawl-like arrangement means the rupee moves within a narrow band around a gradual trend, reflecting RBI's practice of allowing slow depreciation while smoothing sharp moves.

body.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)
body.description: RBI's official data portal for weekly forex reserves, monthly intervention data and balance of payments statistics.

cards.definition: Foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the IMF reserve position held by RBI. $785.7 billion in the week ended 4 September 2026.
Reserves expressed as months of imports they could pay for. About 11 months for India in 2026.
RBI's outstanding commitments to buy or sell dollars on future dates. A record $136.77 billion net short at end of July 2026.
Offsetting the rupee liquidity effect of forex intervention through operations such as bond purchases or swaps.
A change in reported reserves caused by movements in currency or gold prices rather than RBI buying or selling.
IMF classification for a currency kept within a 2% band around a trend for at least six months. India's label since November 2025.

points: India's forex reserves are mostly foreign currency assets, plus gold, SDRs and the IMF reserve position, and cover about 11 months of imports.
Reported reserves change because of both intervention and valuation effects from currency and gold price moves.
RBI uses spot sales, forwards, buy/sell swaps, NDF operations, regulatory curbs and inflow schemes to manage the rupee.
RBI sold a record $53.13 billion net in the spot market in FY26 and built a record $136.77 billion net short forward position by July 2026.
Heavy forward use and the 2026 FCNR(B) swap window explain how reserves hit a record while RBI was defending the rupee.
Headline reserves overstate freely usable reserves when the forward book is large.
RBI smooths volatility rather than defending a level. The IMF classifies India's regime as crawl-like, so intervention levels are speed bumps, not floors.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Reserve, intervention and forward book figures are from RBI releases and market reports as of the dates stated and may be revised. The exchange rate used in the liquidity exercise is illustrative.
